name: Daria Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Daria. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Can you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brookend, which Helen Turner runs with her husband. It's twelve thousand free-range laying hens in mobile sheds that we tow round the fields, plus oilseed rape and wheat. I'm in by six-thirty to open the pop holes, which are the little doors the hens go out through, then it's egg collection, checking water lines, picking up any dead birds and moving fences. I'm still learning the crop side, I nearly sprayed the wrong field in June, which Helen still mentions.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, the tech. The sheds have sensors for temperature and ammonia, and I'm the one who set up the alerts on everyone's phones. I use an AI assistant every day, I got it to help me build a spreadsheet that tracks lay rates by shed. And I film bits of the day for my channel, about four thousand followers, mostly people who like watching chickens run out in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll go through five pictures of the future and ask the same questions for each. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably make a video about it, something like, AI was supposed to take my job and it's still me picking up eggs at six in the morning. People like that kind of thing. At work I'd just say, told you the hens would win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed. I like the tools and I was hoping they'd get much better. But it's fine, I'd still be the person on the farm who knows how they work, and that's worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brookend and grow the channel, maybe try to make it pay a bit, a hundred or two a month from sponsors, egg cartons, feed brands. I'd keep my three-ish months of savings where they are. And I'd finally do the crop spraying certificate so Helen stops bringing up June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like a party that ended early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Helen think of the channel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She pretended to hate it at first, and now she asks how many views the dust bath video got. It sold a few hundred dozen eggs at the farm gate. She's practical, if it works, she's in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in five years, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe running the hen side for Helen, or doing the same somewhere bigger. Or doing the channel properly with some farm consulting on the side. I don't need to pick yet, that's the nice thing about being twenty-seven with no kids.

S0.say: I'd make a video joking that AI was meant to take my job and I'm still picking up eggs at six in the morning. At work I'd say the hens won.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like the tools and hoped they'd improve a lot. I'd still be the person on the farm who knows how they work.
S0.do: Keeps working at the hen farm and tries to earn a hundred or two a month from her farm video channel through sponsors. Takes the crop spraying certificate and leaves her savings as they are.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a party that ended early.
S0.quote: AI was supposed to take my job and it's still me picking up eggs at six in the morning.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is openly disappointed by a quiet future, which is unusual. She already has a small side income from farm videos and a practical boss who backs what works. Her centre outlook shows in a cheerful, no-blame tone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for farms to stop wasting so much time on dull jobs, but people need proper training and a bit of support while they switch. I'd make a video series about trying out the new kit. Honest reviews, not the shiny adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this one's good for me. Egg collection and shed cleaning are the obvious things to automate, and I'd rather be the one who runs it than the one who carries trays. The risk is Helen deciding she only needs one person on the hens, and it's Mick, who's been there twelve years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Helen first, before she goes to me, with a costed plan for an automatic egg collection belt in the two biggest sheds. I'd volunteer to run it and do the dealer's training course. I'd also start using AI to plan the crop rotations, so I'm useful on that side too and not just the chicken girl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Bit guilty about Mick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Mick.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fifty-five, never looked at a screen he didn't sigh at. But he can tell from the sound in a shed if something's wrong, before any sensor. If I'm honest, I'd want him kept on for that, but I can't promise Helen will see it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to Helen before she comes to you. Isn't that risky for a junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's risky either way. If she brings it in and I'm not ready, I'm the cheapest to lose. If I bring it in, I'm the one who knows how it works. I'd rather take the first risk than the second.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance to drop dull farm jobs, as long as people get training and support to switch. I'd make honest video reviews of the new kit, not adverts.
S1.think: This is good for me, because egg collection and shed cleaning are obvious to automate and I'd rather run it than carry trays. The risk is my boss keeping only one person on the hens, and that being the long-serving worker.
S1.do: Takes her boss a costed plan for automatic egg belts in the two biggest sheds and offers to run them after the dealer's course. Uses AI to plan crop rotations so she's useful on the arable side too.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with some guilt about an older colleague.
S1.quote: I'd rather take the first risk than the second.
S1.fieldNote: Daria moves first and frames it as risk management, not ambition. She would bring automation into her own workplace herself. She respected the older worker's skill with sound, which no sensor matches, but was honest that she can't protect him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three all end with full AGI. The only difference is how much time there is. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's way too fast and the government has to put some kind of safety net in, quickly, while things settle. I don't like big promises from politicians, but you can't let everyone drop at once. I'd make a calm video about what farm workers can claim, because people would be panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one rattles me. All my edge comes from being a bit ahead of everyone on the tech, and if the AI does the tech itself, I'm not ahead of anything. Two years is barely enough to get good at one new thing, let alone find something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go all in on whatever's paying for that short window, probably setting up robot systems on other egg farms, because there'd be a rush. I'd save almost everything, maybe live on half my wage and put the rest away. I'd lean on the channel too, because people would want to watch farms change, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but my chest's tight just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd live on half your wage. What goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car upgrade I've been eyeing, eating out with Kezia, my flatmate, and the festival tickets for next summer. I'd keep the gym, because I'd need somewhere to put the stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the channel when robots run the farms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe people still like watching hens, robots or not. Or maybe the AI makes better hen videos than me. I'd find out quickly, I suppose.

S2.say: I'd say it's far too fast and the government must put a safety net in place quickly. I'd make a calm video explaining what farm workers can claim, because people would be panicking.
S2.think: This one rattles me, because my edge comes from being ahead on tech, and if AI handles the tech itself I'm not ahead of anything. Two years is barely enough to master one new thing.
S2.do: Takes short-term work installing robot systems on other egg farms during the rush and lives on half her wage, saving the rest. Leans on her video channel for extra income while interest lasts.
S2.feel: Anxious with a tight chest, though not frozen.
S2.quote: If the AI does the tech itself, I'm not ahead of anything.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Daria's confidence cracks: her advantage depends on being ahead, and fast AGI removes that. She still moves quickly, grabbing the short installation boom. Her honesty about not knowing whether her channel survives was striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, but with five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a sensible plan, a bit of support, some retraining money, and businesses being honest about what they're bringing in. No need for drama. I'd probably do a video series on it, how to get ready if you work on a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years suits me. I'd be one of the people helping other farms switch for the first few years, which pays well, and I'd have time to build something of my own. I'd still be nervous about the end, but I'd have savings and options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an agricultural engineering course part-time in year one, and start doing setup work for other farms on weekends. I'd put some savings into a small share of a drone spraying business my friend Sana is starting, if her numbers stack up. And the channel would become more of a how-to, which might actually earn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. More like the night before a big job than the night before bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting savings into Sana's business is a risk. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a third of what I've got, so about a month's money. I'd look at her numbers properly first, with the AI and with my uncle who does accounts. If it goes wrong, I've lost a month, not my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change course in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the robots getting good at the setup work too. That'd be my cue to stop installing and go further, maybe into the business side, helping farms decide what to buy. I'd keep checking every few months.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a sensible plan with some support, retraining money and honesty from businesses, without drama. I'd make a video series on getting ready.
S3.think: Five years suits me, because helping farms switch would pay well early on and I'd have time to build something of my own. I'd still be nervous about the end, but I'd have savings and options.
S3.do: Starts a part-time agricultural engineering course and weekend setup work for other farms in the first year. Invests about a month's money in a friend's drone spraying business after checking the numbers.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, like the night before a big job.
S3.quote: If it goes wrong, I've lost a month, not my flat.
S3.fieldNote: Daria thinks in measured bets: a third of her savings, numbers checked twice. She already plans to watch for signs that even setup work is automating and pivot again. The extra time turns her anxiety into busyness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to get ready, so let's be grown-ups about it. Some help for those who need it, and lots of freedom for people to try new things. I'd be cheerful about it in public, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. I'd have a decade to build a business, save, and learn, and I'd only be thirty-seven at the end. If robots make food and energy cheap, a bit of savings might go a long way. I'm not scared of this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job at Brookend for a few years and run the egg belt project I talked about. Then I'd go out on my own, helping small farms automate, with the channel as my shop window. I'd put money into the business and into a pension, which I've never thought about before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, really. I'd like to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd like to see it. Is there any part that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick, again, and people like my dad, who's a bus driver and fifty-eight. I'd be fine, but I'd be the one at Christmas being told it's all right for you. That'd sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd help him, properly, with money if I had it. He'd hate that, he's proud. Maybe I'd frame it as hiring him to drive my van.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty to get ready, so we should be grown-ups about it with help for those who need it and freedom to try new things. I'd be cheerful about it in public.
S4.think: I'd probably do well, with a decade to build a business, save and learn and still only be thirty-seven. If robots make food and energy cheap, some savings could go a long way.
S4.do: Keeps her farm job for a few years to run the egg belt project, then starts her own business helping small farms automate, using her channel for publicity. Invests in the business and starts a pension.
S4.feel: Calm and curious, wanting to see it happen.
S4.quote: I'd be the one at Christmas being told it's all right for you. That'd sting.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Daria is openly optimistic and plans a business built on the change itself. Her worry turns to her father, a bus driver near retirement, and to the family tension of doing well while others don't. The idea of hiring him to drive her van was a kind, practical touch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My whole thing is being early, and two years is too fast for anyone to be early. What would help is a basic safety net that kicks in fast and doesn't make you fill in forty forms, and help with starting a small business, like a loan you don't pay back until you're earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people like me make it worse. I'm the one who'd bring the egg belt in. I think about that more than I let on. Someone's going to do it, but it's weird when it's you.

headlineQuote: Someone's going to do it, but it's weird when it's you.
portrait: Daria Zhang is a 27-year-old junior worker at Brookend, a free-range egg and arable farm, who sets up the shed sensors, uses AI every day and runs a small farm video channel, while still learning the crop side. She is single, shares a flat with a nurse friend and has about three months saved. She would be calm, even a little disappointed, if AI stalled, and with steady change she would bring automation to her own farm before her boss could. Fast AGI rattles her because her edge is being ahead, but with five or ten years she makes measured bets and plans her own automation business. She worries about older colleagues and her bus-driver father, and quietly about being the one who brings the machines in.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her strength is being early and two years is too fast for anyone to be early.
whatWouldHelp: A fast, simple safety net without endless forms, and help starting a small business, such as a loan repaid only once she is earning.
